Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 105, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah al-Fil.

It is Meccan.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ Al-Fil (the elephant) is a well-known animal. The meaning of His words ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is: Do you not know? It has also been said: Have you not seen the traces of what your Lord did to the companions of the elephant? The companions of the elephant were a army from the Abyssinians (al-Habasha), whose commander was Abraha ibn al-Sabah, Abu Yaksum; and it has been said: someone else.

They attacked the Ka'bah, intending to destroy and demolish it. The most sound account reported about its cause is that Abraha was a Christian who built a church (bay'ah) in Sana'a in Yemen, adorned it with the finest garments and jewels, and said: "I have built this so that the Arabs will make pilgrimage to it, instead of the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah." He ordered the people to do so and compelled them to it. A man from the Arabs came—it has been said that he was from the Banu Kinanah—entered the church, defiled it, and fled. This was reported to Abraha, who became extremely angry and swore by Christianity and the Messiah that he would certainly attack the Ka'bah and demolish it stone by stone. Then he attacked the Ka'bah with a great army.

There is a lengthy story concerning this. He brought with him an elephant called Mahmud; it has been said that there were eight elephants, the largest of which was this one. On the way he encountered a force of Arabs, defeated them, and killed many of them, until he reached al-Ta'if. Then he set out from al-Ta'if toward Mecca, with Abu Righal as his guide. Abu Righal died on the way, and his grave is the one the Arabs stone; it lies between Mecca and al-Ta'if. Abraha and the army halted at al-Mughammas. The people of Mecca heard of this, and their leader at that time was Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim. The army raided whatever property and camels of the people of Mecca they found, and they seized two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib. Then Abd al-Muttalib came to Abraha seeking his camels—he was a tall and handsome man. When Abraha saw him, he was impressed by his good looks and bearing, and said: "What is your need?" He said: "That you return my camels."

Abraha said to his interpreter: "Tell him: I was impressed by what I saw of your appearance, but then I lost interest in you when I heard your speech." Abd al-Muttalib said: "What has caused the king to lose interest in me?" He replied: "I came to demolish your honour and the honour of your forefathers, yet you did not mention it, and you asked me about camels I had taken from you!" Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." So he ordered the camels returned to him. Abd al-Muttalib went back and ordered the people of Mecca to disperse to the mountain tops, saying: "A calamity has come upon you for which you have no power."

Then Abd al-Muttalib took hold of the ring of the Ka'bah and said:

(O Lord, I do not hope for them other than You... O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.)

(Indeed the enemy of the House is the enemy of You.)

It is also well known that he said:

(O Lord, a man defends his household... so defend Your sanctuary.)

(Let not their cross and their might ever overcome Your might.)

Al-mihal means punishment.

(If You are leaving them and our Ka'bah... then do as You see fit.)

Then he went out with the people and they left Mecca. It is related that the elephant, whenever it sensed being turned toward Mecca, refused, but whenever it was turned toward Yemen it hastened and ran. Allah held the elephant back from the House. This is the meaning of what is established from the Prophet ﷺ, that on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, when his she-camel al-Qaswa' knelt down and the people said, "al-Qaswa' has become stubborn," the Prophet ﷺ said: "No, but the One who held back the elephant has held her back."

Then Allah sent against them birds coming from the direction of the sea. Ibn Abbas said: they had the beaks of birds and the snouts of dogs. It has been said: they were black; it has been said: they were red. With each bird were three stones: two stones in its claws and one in its beak. In the account it is said that the stone was smaller than a chickpea and larger than a lentil. The birds came and pelted them with the stones. In the account it is also said that the stone would strike a man's head and come out of his rear, and he would fall and die; and if it fell on one side of a man, it would come out the other side. The people fled and fell dead along the road.

It has also been said: when a stone struck one of them, the place was pierced with pustules and he was afflicted with smallpox; this was the first time smallpox was seen in the lands of the Arabs. And Allah knows best.

As for Abraha, he fell apart along the road, joint by joint. Then his chest split open from his heart, and he died.

The Year of the Elephant is the year in which the Prophet ﷺ was born. It has also been said that he was born two years after that, but the correct view is the first. The people of knowledge said: that event was a preparation (irhas) for the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ and a foundation for it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ That is: He nullified their scheming and their effort. It is also said that His words ﴿in going astray﴾ mean that it went astray from them, and they failed to attain what they had intended.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 105, verse 3:

And His saying: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks (ababil)﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Groups, in dispersion." According to Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra': it has no singular. According to al-Kisa'i: its singular is abūl, like ajājīl and ajūl.

It is also said: ﴿tayran ababil﴾ means: many. It is also said: flocks, following one another.

And His saying: ﴿Casting at them stones of baked clay﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: sijjil (سجيل) in Persian is (sang-gil), i.e., clay (gil) of stone (sang). It is also said: "of sijjil" means from the sky, and it is the name of the lowest heaven (samaʾ al-dunya).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 105, verse 5:

And His saying: ﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾. The ʿaṣf (stalk, chaff) is the leaf of the crop. Its meaning: like a stalk whose contents have been eaten. It was also said: all of its produce.

The meaning is that God, exalted is He, likened them to the crop that the beasts had eaten, trampled and scattered, so that nothing of it remained. Thus He likened their destruction to that. And God knows best.
